newsitem.title: UGANDA: Iranian leader to mediate in Uganda-Sudan conflict.
newsitem.headline: Iranian leader to mediate in Uganda-Sudan conflict.

text.p: Iranian President Hashemi Rafsanjani left Uganda for the Sudan on Sunday on his six-nation African tour, saying he would try to mediate in disputes between Uganda and the Sudan.

Rafsanjani told a news conference at the end of his four-day visit to Uganda that he had discussed the conflict between the two neighbours with Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni and would try to find a solution to it.
"We need general agreement to bring this conflict to an end," the Iranian leader said.
"Sudan and Uganda have agreed upon this and my visit to Sudan should help us find a peaceful end to this problem," he told reporters in Kampala.
Sudan accuses Uganda of backing rebels fighting a 13-year-old insurgency in the country's south, while Uganda accuses the Sudan of aiding Ugandan Christian fundamentalist rebels in its north.
Diplomats and journalists in the region say there is some truth in both accusations and say disagreements between the two states have fuelled the two insurgencies.
Rafsanjani said Museveni had agreed to his mediation efforts, as had the Islamist rulers in Sudan.
"Considering that there is goodwill from both sides, we hope that this problem will be settled," he told a news conference attended by Museveni and senior members of his government.

The SPLA have fought since 1983 against what they say is domination of the mainly Christian and animist south by the Islamised Arab regime in Khartoum. The Lord's Resistance Army (LRA) has waged a guerrilla war in northern Uganda since 1987, saying it wants to remove Museveni's 10-year-old government and rule Uganda in line with the Bible's 10 Commandments.

During Rafsanjani's visit, Uganda and Iran signed a memoranda of understanding for economic cooperation, and agreed to exchange diplomatic missions, establish airline links and cooperate in agricultural research, officials said.

Iran's national airline would start flights into Uganda, and details of boosting trade between the two countries would be worked out soon, communiques signed at the end of Rafsanjani's four-day visit said.

Iran said it would help cash-strapped Uganda to harness its water resources by building electricity generation plants along the Nile to help ease a chronic power shortage that is stalling economic growth.
"We believe the right thing is for African countries to construct themselves and delink themselves from the chains of imperialism," Rafsanjani said.
"The interest of those imperialist forces is to see that African countries remain backward so they can exploit them," he added, speaking through an interpreter.
Rafsanjani, who was in Kenya last week, is due to visit South Africa, Zimbabwe and Tanzania later on his African tour.
